title: General Ecology
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 200L General Ecology curriculum: ecosystem structure, energy flow, biogeochemical cycles, population and community ecology, succession, biomes, and abiotic/biotic interactions.

questions.question: Ecology is best defined as the scientific study of:
options: The interactions between organisms and their environment
The internal anatomy of organisms only
The classification of organisms into taxonomic groups
The genetic code of living things
questions.correct_answer: The interactions between organisms and their environment
questions.explanation: Ecology studies how organisms relate to one another and to the physical (abiotic) and biological (biotic) components of their surroundings.

questions.question: The study of the ecology of a single species and its relationship with the environment is called:
questions.explanation: Autecology focuses on an individual species' relationship to environmental factors, in contrast to synecology, which studies whole communities.

questions.question: An ecosystem is defined as:
options: A community of organisms interacting with each other and with their non-living (abiotic) environment as a functional unit
A single population of one species
The non-living components of the environment only
A group of related species sharing a common ancestor
questions.correct_answer: A community of organisms interacting with each other and with their non-living (abiotic) environment as a functional unit
questions.explanation: An ecosystem includes both the biotic community and the abiotic environment, linked through energy flow and nutrient cycling.

questions.question: The specific physical place where an organism lives is called its:
questions.explanation: Habitat refers to the actual physical location or environment an organism occupies, whereas niche describes its functional role within that habitat.

questions.question: An organism's ecological niche refers to:
options: Its functional role in the ecosystem, including how it obtains resources and interacts with other species
Only the geographic location where it is found
The temperature range of its habitat only
questions.correct_answer: Its functional role in the ecosystem, including how it obtains resources and interacts with other species
questions.explanation: Niche encompasses all the biotic and abiotic conditions and resources an organism needs to survive and reproduce, and its functional role within the community.

questions.question: The difference between an organism's fundamental niche and its realised niche is that the realised niche:
options: Is the portion of the fundamental niche actually occupied due to competition and other biotic interactions
Is always larger than the fundamental niche
questions.correct_answer: Is the portion of the fundamental niche actually occupied due to competition and other biotic interactions
questions.explanation: The fundamental niche is the full range of conditions a species could theoretically occupy, while the realised niche is narrower due to competitive exclusion and other biological constraints.

questions.question: A sequence of organisms in which each is eaten by the next member, transferring energy along the sequence, is called a:
questions.explanation: A food chain is a single, linear pathway of energy transfer, e.g., grass to grasshopper to frog to snake.

questions.question: An interconnected network of multiple overlapping food chains within a community is called a:
questions.explanation: A food web represents the complex network of feeding relationships that occur when multiple food chains interconnect within an ecosystem.

questions.question: Organisms that manufacture their own food using light or chemical energy, such as green plants, are called:
questions.explanation: Producers, mainly green plants and algae, convert inorganic materials into organic compounds via photosynthesis, forming the base of most food chains.

questions.question: According to the ten percent law of energy transfer, when energy passes from one trophic level to the next, approximately:
options: Only about 10% of the energy is transferred to the next level, the rest being lost mainly as heat
All the energy is transferred with no loss
Energy transfer is unrelated to trophic level
questions.correct_answer: Only about 10% of the energy is transferred to the next level, the rest being lost mainly as heat
questions.explanation: The ten percent law reflects that most energy at each trophic level is lost as metabolic heat, used in respiration, or not consumed, so only roughly a tenth passes to the next level.

questions.question: Organisms such as fungi and bacteria that break down dead organic matter, releasing nutrients back into the ecosystem, are called:
questions.explanation: Decomposers (saprotrophs) break down dead organisms and waste products, recycling nutrients back into the abiotic environment for reuse by producers.

questions.question: An ecological pyramid that can sometimes show an inverted shape (e.g., in some aquatic ecosystems) because a few large producers support many small consumers is the pyramid of:
options: Biomass at a fixed moment in some cases
Both numbers and biomass, depending on the ecosystem
questions.correct_answer: Both numbers and biomass, depending on the ecosystem
questions.explanation: Pyramids of numbers and biomass can be inverted in certain systems (e.g., one large tree supporting many insects, or phytoplankton with fast turnover supporting more zooplankton biomass), while the pyramid of energy is always upright due to the second law of thermodynamics.

questions.question: The pyramid of energy in any ecosystem is always upright (never inverted) because:
options: Energy is progressively lost as heat at each trophic level, so less energy is available at higher levels
Energy cannot be created or destroyed
All organisms respire at the same rate
questions.correct_answer: Energy is progressively lost as heat at each trophic level, so less energy is available at higher levels
questions.explanation: Because energy dissipates as heat during metabolism at every transfer, the amount available strictly decreases up the trophic levels, so the energy pyramid is always upright.

questions.question: The continuous movement of carbon between the atmosphere, living organisms, oceans, and rocks is known as the:
questions.explanation: The carbon cycle traces carbon through photosynthesis (fixation), respiration, decomposition, combustion, and long-term storage in rocks and fossil fuels.

questions.question: In the nitrogen cycle, the conversion of atmospheric nitrogen gas (N2) into ammonia, usable by plants, is called:
questions.explanation: Nitrogen fixation, carried out by bacteria such as Rhizobium and Azotobacter (and some cyanobacteria), converts inert atmospheric N2 into biologically usable ammonia.

questions.question: The process by which nitrifying bacteria convert ammonia into nitrite and then nitrate is called:
questions.explanation: Nitrification is a two-step oxidation carried out by bacteria (e.g. Nitrosomonas converting ammonia to nitrite, Nitrobacter converting nitrite to nitrate), producing the nitrate form most readily absorbed by plant roots.

questions.question: Denitrifying bacteria contribute to the nitrogen cycle by:
options: Converting nitrate back into atmospheric nitrogen gas, completing the cycle
Absorbing nitrogen directly for plant use
questions.correct_answer: Converting nitrate back into atmospheric nitrogen gas, completing the cycle
questions.explanation: Denitrification, carried out under anaerobic conditions by bacteria such as Pseudomonas, reduces nitrate back to gaseous nitrogen, returning it to the atmosphere.

questions.question: The phosphorus cycle is distinct from the carbon and nitrogen cycles in that it:
options: Has no significant gaseous phase and cycles mainly through rocks, soil, and water
Requires photosynthesis as its sole driving process
questions.correct_answer: Has no significant gaseous phase and cycles mainly through rocks, soil, and water
questions.explanation: Unlike carbon and nitrogen, phosphorus lacks a significant atmospheric gas phase; it is released mainly through the weathering of phosphate-bearing rocks and cycles through soil, water and living organisms.

questions.question: A population growth curve that shows an initial slow increase, followed by a rapid exponential rise, and finally levelling off near the environment's carrying capacity is described as:
questions.explanation: Logistic (sigmoid) growth reflects a population that slows as it approaches the carrying capacity of its environment due to resource limitation and increased competition.

questions.question: A J-shaped population growth curve reflects:
options: Unrestricted exponential growth with no immediate limiting factor
Growth that levels off at carrying capacity
questions.correct_answer: Unrestricted exponential growth with no immediate limiting factor
questions.explanation: J-shaped (exponential) growth occurs when resources are effectively unlimited, allowing the population to increase at a constant, ever-accelerating rate before eventually crashing or being checked.

questions.question: The maximum population size that a given environment can sustainably support with available resources is called the:
questions.explanation: Carrying capacity (K) is the upper limit of population size an environment can support long-term, given its available resources such as food, space and water.

questions.question: The gradual, orderly, and predictable change in the species composition of a community over time in a given area is called:
questions.explanation: Succession describes the sequential replacement of communities over time in an area, driven by changing environmental conditions created by the organisms themselves.

questions.question: Primary succession differs from secondary succession in that primary succession:
options: Begins on a bare substrate lacking any previous soil or living organisms, such as bare rock or new volcanic land
Always occurs faster than secondary succession
Starts on soil that already contains seeds and organic matter from a prior community
questions.correct_answer: Begins on a bare substrate lacking any previous soil or living organisms, such as bare rock or new volcanic land
questions.explanation: Primary succession starts from essentially lifeless substrates with no soil, such as bare rock, requiring pioneer species to initiate soil formation, unlike secondary succession which begins on previously vegetated, disturbed land.

questions.question: The relatively stable, self-perpetuating final community that results at the end of a successional sequence is called the:
questions.explanation: The climax community is the stable end-point of succession, in equilibrium with the prevailing environmental conditions, persisting until a major disturbance occurs.

questions.question: The first organisms to colonise a bare, previously uninhabited area during primary succession are called:
questions.explanation: Pioneer species, such as lichens and mosses on bare rock, are hardy colonisers that begin soil formation and modify conditions to allow later successional species to establish.

questions.question: A close, mutually beneficial relationship between two different species, in which both partners benefit, is termed:
questions.explanation: Mutualism is a symbiotic relationship in which both interacting species derive benefit, such as the nitrogen-fixing relationship between Rhizobium bacteria and legume roots.

questions.question: A relationship in which one species benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed is called:
questions.explanation: In commensalism, one organism gains a benefit (e.g., shelter or transport) while the other partner experiences no significant effect, such as an epiphytic orchid growing on a tree branch.

questions.question: Competition between individuals of the same species for a limited resource is referred to as:
questions.explanation: Intraspecific competition occurs among members of the same species, generally more intense than interspecific competition because they share identical resource requirements.

questions.question: Liebig's Law of the Minimum states that:
options: The growth of an organism is limited by the single essential resource in shortest supply relative to its need, not by the total amount of resources available
All resources are equally limiting at all times
Only temperature can limit plant growth
Organisms are unaffected by resource scarcity
questions.correct_answer: The growth of an organism is limited by the single essential resource in shortest supply relative to its need, not by the total amount of resources available
questions.explanation: Liebig's Law identifies growth-limiting factors as whichever essential nutrient or resource is scarcest relative to an organism's requirement, even if other resources are abundant.

questions.question: Plants adapted to survive in very dry (arid) habitats, often with thick cuticles, reduced leaves, and water-storing tissue, are called:
questions.explanation: Xerophytes possess structural and physiological adaptations, such as sunken stomata, thick cuticles, and succulent tissue, to minimise water loss in dry environments.

questions.question: Plants specially adapted to live fully or partly submerged in water, such as water lilies, are known as:
questions.explanation: Hydrophytes are adapted to aquatic environments, often with air-filled tissues (aerenchyma) for buoyancy and reduced or absent cuticle/stomatal control since water is not limiting.

questions.question: Plants adapted to tolerate high soil or water salinity, commonly found in mangrove swamps and salt marshes, are called:
questions.explanation: Halophytes have physiological adaptations, such as salt-excreting glands or salt-tolerant cell osmotic mechanisms, allowing them to grow in saline environments like mangroves.

questions.question: A large-scale ecological region characterised by a distinct climate and dominant vegetation type, such as tropical rainforest or savanna, is called a:
questions.explanation: A biome is a major regional ecological community defined largely by its climate and the characteristic vegetation and animal life it supports, e.g., tropical rainforest, savanna, desert, or tundra.

questions.question: The West African tropical rainforest biome is generally characterised by:
options: High rainfall throughout most of the year, high temperatures, and a multi-layered (stratified) canopy of tall broadleaf evergreen trees
Very low and unpredictable rainfall with sparse, drought-adapted vegetation
Permanently frozen soil and stunted vegetation
Grass-dominated vegetation with scattered drought-resistant trees
questions.correct_answer: High rainfall throughout most of the year, high temperatures, and a multi-layered (stratified) canopy of tall broadleaf evergreen trees
questions.explanation: Tropical rainforests are distinguished by consistently high rainfall and temperature, supporting a highly diverse, vertically stratified community of evergreen trees.

questions.question: A transitional zone of overlap between two distinct adjacent communities or ecosystems, often showing greater species diversity than either community alone, is called an:
questions.explanation: An ecotone is a boundary zone where two communities meet and blend, often exhibiting an 'edge effect' with higher species diversity due to the mix of conditions and resources from both sides.

questions.question: Net Primary Productivity (NPP) of an ecosystem is calculated as:
options: Gross Primary Productivity minus the energy used by producers in respiration
The rate of decomposition of organic matter
questions.correct_answer: Gross Primary Productivity minus the energy used by producers in respiration
questions.explanation: NPP = GPP - R, representing the energy actually available for growth and available to be passed on to consumers, after producers have used some energy for their own respiration.

questions.question: Edaphic factors, which influence plant distribution in an ecosystem, refer to:
options: Soil-related factors such as texture, pH, nutrient content, and moisture
questions.correct_answer: Soil-related factors such as texture, pH, nutrient content, and moisture
questions.explanation: Edaphic factors are the physical and chemical properties of soil (structure, texture, pH, mineral content, water-holding capacity) that influence which plants can grow in an area.
